page: Microsoft Azure M64 is a memory-optimized virtual machine from the MS family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 64 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 32 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 8280M processor operating at 2.7 GHz. The x86_64 architecture includes 32 KB L1d, 1.0 MB L2, and 38 MB L3 cache. It supports AVX, AVX-512, AES, BMI2, ADX, and FMA instruction sets. The server is equipped with 1024.0 GB of RAM, providing 16.0 GB of memory per core, and includes 7340 GB of local storage. No GPUs are present on this instance.

Benchmark data indicates a clear contrast between single-core and multi-core performance. Single-core metrics, such as stress-ng single-core CPU performance, Geekbench single-core score, and single-threaded gzip or bzip3 operations, consistently fall into the bottom 10%. However, multi-core capabilities are more robust, with stress-ng multi-core, Geekbench multi-core, and PassMark CPU scores ranking in the middle 50%. Notably, uncached read-only memory bandwidth for large blocks (256MB) and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression show strong performance, placing in the top 25%. Large-block write memory bandwidth and database operations remain in the average tier.

Given its high memory density of 16.0 GB per vCPU and substantial 7340 GB local storage, the M64 is qualitatively structured for memory-intensive enterprise workloads. It is well-suited for large-scale databases, in-memory caching, and data-intensive processing where multi-threaded memory bandwidth is critical. However, its weak single-core performance and poor text-generation speeds for large language models make it less suitable for latency-sensitive single-threaded tasks or intensive AI inference workloads.

Built on the x86_64 architecture and managed via Microsoft Hyper-V, it features a massive 1024.0 GB of RAM alongside 7340 GB of local storage, with no integrated GPUs. Performance benchmarks reveal a significant divergence: single-core CPU execution and single-threaded compression tasks rank in the bottom 10%, whereas multi-core processing and large-block uncached read memory bandwidth achieve strong results in the top 25%. This hardware profile offers high resource density for memory-bound applications. It is highly suited for large-scale databases, in-memory data processing, and multi-threaded enterprise workloads, though it is less optimal for single-threaded or AI inference tasks.
